en: The Parivāra:
The Analysis of the Bhikkhunī Rules,
Second Part
2.9 Chapter on the Formulation of Rules (Katthapaññattivāra) 1. Section on Defeat (Pārājikakaṇḍa):
Where was the offense of defeat formulated by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—concerning the intentional touching of a body?
Concerning whom?
Concerning what matter? ...
By whom was it brought?
Where was this offense of defeat (pārājika) formulated by the Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—concerning the consent to physical contact?
It was formulated at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā. On what basis?
On the basis that the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā, being lustful, consented to physical contact with a lustful man; on that basis.
Is there therein a formal rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), and a rule for what has not yet arisen (anuppannapaññatti)?
There is one formal rule;
there is no supplementary rule or rule for what has not yet arisen therein.
Is it a universal promulgation or a partial promulgation?
It is a universal promulgation.
Is it a common promulgation or an uncommon promulgation?
Is it an uncommon designation?
Is it a designation from one side or a designation from both sides?
It is a designation from one side.
In which of the four recitations of the Pātimokkha is it included, and in which is it contained?
Is it included in the Nidāna and contained in the Nidāna?
By which recitation does it come to be recited?
It comes under the heading by the second summary.
Of the four failures, which failure is it?
It is failure in virtue.
Of the seven classes of offenses, which class of offense is it?
It is the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika).
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
It originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, not from speech …pe… From whom was this brought?
Handed down in succession:
Upāli, Dāsaka,
and likewise Soṇaka and Siggava.
With Moggaliputta as the fifth,
these [councils] took place in the land named Jambusiri.
…pe…
These Nāgas of great wisdom,
knowers of the Vinaya and experts in the Path,
proclaimed the Vinaya on the island of Dīpa.
The Piṭaka of Tambapaṇṇi.
Where was the Pārājika offense regarding the concealment of a fault (vajjappaṭicchādana) prescribed?
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
In regard to what matter?
The nun Thullanandā, knowing that a nun had committed an offense entailing defeat, neither reproved her herself nor informed the community regarding that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin: [that which arises from] concealment.
Regarding the laying down of the burden...
[and so on] ...on account of not relinquishing after being pressed three times, where was the offense entailing expulsion (pārājika) laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
In regard to what matter?
The nun Thullanandā followed the monk Ariṭṭha—who had previously been a vulture-trainer and had been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha—with respect to that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin: [namely, from a deliberate act].
Regarding the laying down of the burden... [etc.
...The eighth case: in what place was the offense entailing defeat (pārājika) laid down on account of the fulfillment of the matter?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six bhikkhunīs.
In regard to what matter?
The group of six bhikkhunīs fulfilled the eighth offense in that matter.
There is one rule.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin: [the origin of what is done unintentionally].
... [regarding] the laying down of the burden ... [as above].
The offenses involving defeat (pārājika) are concluded.
2. The Section on the Saṅghādisesa Offenses, etc.

Where was this *saṅghādisesa* offense prescribed by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—concerning a nun who brings a lawsuit for the purpose of instigating a legal dispute?
With reference to whom?
On account of what matter? …pe…
By whom was it brought forth?
By the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—this Saṅghādisesa rule was laid down on account of a nun who brought a legal case as a litigant.
Where was it laid down? It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
In regard to what matter?
The nun Thullanandā lived as one who brought false accusations; this was the case.
Is there therein a formal rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), or a rule for an unarisen offense (anuppannapaññatti)?
There is one formal rule.
Therein, there is no subsequent rule (anupaññatti) nor a newly arisen rule (anuppannapaññatti).
Is it a universal rule (sabbatthapaññatti) or a partial rule (padesapaññatti)?
It is a universal rule.
Is it a common designation or an uncommon designation?
It is an uncommon designation.
Is it a designation from one side or a designation from both sides?
A single designation.
In which of the four recitations of the Pātimokkha is it included, and in which is it contained?
It is included in the Introduction (Nidāna) and contained within the Introduction.
By which summary does it come under a summary?
It comes under the third summary.
Of the four failures, which failure is it?
Failure in virtue.
Among the seven classes of offenses, to which class does it belong? It belongs to the class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Sangha (*saṅghādisesa*).
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
It originates by two origins:
it may originate from both body and speech, but not from mind.
It may originate from body, speech, and mind …pe… From whom was it brought?
It was brought down through oral tradition.
Upāli, Dāsaka,
Soṇaka, and likewise Siggava;
with Moggaliputta as the fifth—
These, in the land called Jambusiri...
[etc.
...these Nāgas of great wisdom.
Knowing the Vinaya and skilled in the Path,
they proclaimed the Vinaya Pitaka on Tambapaṇṇi.
Where was the Saṅghādisesa offense concerning the ordination of a *cori* (a runaway slave) laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā. On what basis?
On the basis that the bhikkhunī Thullanandā gave the full admission to a female thief. On that basis.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins:
it may originate from speech and mind, but not from body.
It may arise from body, speech, and mind … [as before] … Where was the first Saṅghādisesa offense regarding traveling to another village established?
It was established at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a certain bhikkhunī.
In regard to what matter?
A certain bhikkhunī went alone from one village to another; this is the basis for the rule. There is one original formulation (paññatti) and three subsequent formulations (anupaññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin: the offense of wrong-doing (dubbhāsita).
In the first *pārājika*... [etc.

... Regarding the offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*) for reinstating a nun who has been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, without having obtained the consent of the Saṅgha that performed the act and without knowing the will of the group:
where was it laid down? It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
On account of what matter?

The nun Thullanandā reinstated a nun who had been suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, without having obtained the permission of the Saṅgha that performed the act and without knowing the consent of the group. This is the case regarding that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin: [namely,] from a deliberate action.
Regarding the laying down of the burden...

[as before] ...On what account was the Saṅghādisesa offense prescribed for a lustful bhikkhunī who, having received with her own hand from the hand of a lustful man, eats either solid food or soft food?
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Sundarīnandā.
On account of what matter?
The nun Sundarīnandā, being lustful, accepted food from the hand of a lustful man; this is the matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin: [the offense of intentional lying].
In the first *pārājika*...
[as before] ... "Noble lady, what can this man do to you, whether he be lustful or free from lust, since you yourself are free from lust?
Come now, noble lady, whatever fresh or cooked food this man gives you, take it with your own hand..."
"Having accepted it, eat or consume it"—where was this Saṅghādisesa offense, concerning the condition of incitement, laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning a certain bhikkhunī.
In what matter? A certain bhikkhunī said:
“What can this man do to you, noble lady, whether he be lustful or free from lust?”

Or, because you are free from lust: "Come now, noble lady, having received with your own hand whatever fresh or cooked food this man gives you, eat it or consume it"—if she encourages him in this way, that is the basis for the offense.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).

Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [as before] … On account of not relinquishing [an offense] when a bhikkhunī who is angry and displeased has been pressed up to the third time, an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa) was laid down where?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī.
In regard to what matter?
The bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī, being angry and displeased, spoke thus: “I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dhamma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the training. This is the basis for the offense.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin: [that which originates from a deliberate action].
Regarding the laying down of the burden...
[as before]... In what place was the Saṅghādisesa rule laid down on account of a nun who, having been accused in some legal matter, did not desist after being formally admonished up to three times?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī.
In regard to what matter?
On a certain legal issue, the bhikkhunī Caṇḍakāḷī, being contradicted, became angry and displeased, and she spoke thus:
“The bhikkhunīs act out of favoritism; the bhikkhunīs act out of ill will; the bhikkhunīs act out of delusion;
the bhikkhunīs act out of fear. This was the basis for the offense.
There is one classification.
It originates from one of the six origins of offenses—namely, by laying down the burden ... [and so forth] ... .
Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense prescribed for not desisting after being admonished up to three times by bhikkhunīs who are associating with [laypeople]?
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning a number of bhikkhunīs.
On what basis? On the basis that a number of bhikkhunīs were living in close association. On that basis.
There is one classification.
It originates from one of the six origins of offenses—
namely, by laying down the burden … [and so forth] … .

“Venerable ladies, you should live in association; do not live apart”—regarding her who, despite being exhorted up to three times with formal admonition, did not desist from this, for what reason was this Saṅghādisesa rule laid down? It was laid down at Sāvatthī. With reference to whom? With reference to the group of six bhikkhunīs. What was the offense? Insulting speech. What was the cause? Living apart. What was the result? Concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā. On what basis?
On the basis that the bhikkhunī Thullanandā urged [them], saying: "Venerable ladies, you should dwell in association; do not dwell apart. It was on this basis.

through relinquishing the burden (*dhuranikkhepa*) ... [and so forth] ... .
Where was the offense entailing confession prescribed for eating curd after having requested it?
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom was it prescribed?
Concerning the group of six bhikkhunīs.
With reference to what matter?
Concerning the matter that the group of six bhikkhunīs requested curd and then consumed it.
One is a primary rule (paññatti), one is a supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from four origins ... [as above] ...
The first section on the rules of promulgation is finished.
